title: Nitrogen recommendation context
text: Nitrogen recommendations should be tied to crop, realistic yield goal, soil organic matter, manure or legume credits, nitrate risk, timing, placement, and local calibration. If a recent soil test or yield goal is missing, ask for it before giving a rate.

title: Phosphorus and potassium interpretation
text: Phosphorus and potassium advice depends on soil-test method, critical levels, pH, crop removal, placement, and local calibration curves. Bray, Olsen, and Mehlich values are not interchangeable without calibration.

title: Label-bound product advice
text: A pesticide recommendation requires crop and site, target pest or weed, geography or registration context, crop stage, application method, buffers, resistance-management constraints, and the current product label. Without those, stay at decision-framework or mode-of-action level.

title: Spray weather window checks
text: Spray timing should consider wind speed and direction, gusts, temperature inversion risk, rainfast interval, temperature restrictions, drift buffers, sensitive downwind crops, drainage ditches or water bodies, rainfall-driven runoff risk, and label-specific requirements. Do not treat a buffer as enough when runoff could move product toward water; check the current label, field slope, drainage path, and forecast before spraying.

title: Herbicide resistance stewardship
text: Resistance management combines correct identification, effective sites of action, multiple effective modes where allowed, residual layering, nonchemical tactics, scouting escapes, and rotating crops or tactics across seasons.

title: Soybean iron deficiency chlorosis
text: Iron deficiency chlorosis risk rises with high pH, carbonate or bicarbonate, wet or compacted soils, salinity, nitrate, and susceptible varieties. Management emphasizes tolerant varieties, drainage and compaction correction, seeding-rate adjustments, and in-furrow chelate where locally validated.

title: Corn gray leaf spot triage
text: Gray leaf spot often shows rectangular lesions bounded by leaf veins. Fungicide decisions should consider hybrid susceptibility, disease severity on upper leaves, crop growth stage, weather favorability, yield potential, and local threshold guidance.

title: Aphid threshold framing
text: Insecticide decisions for aphids should start with scouting counts, crop stage, trend over repeated visits, natural enemies, plant stress, and regional economic thresholds. Avoid product selection without crop, pest species, threshold, and label context.

title: Variable-rate prescription workflow
text: A variable-rate workflow should validate boundaries, clean yield maps, remove outlier passes, align multi-year layers, combine soil tests and soil EC or imagery, define stable management zones, ground-truth zones, and preserve an audit trail from data to prescription.

title: Corn nitrogen assessment after heavy rain
text: Before changing a corn sidedress nitrogen plan after heavy rain, verify how much nitrogen was applied, its source, timing and placement, whether a nitrification inhibitor was used, rainfall amount, how long the soil stayed saturated, soil temperature, soil texture and drainage, crop stage and current yield potential, and any manure or previous-crop credits. Heavy rain does not prove that a fixed amount of nitrogen was lost. Loss risk depends on how much applied nitrogen had converted to nitrate, whether saturated conditions favored denitrification, whether water moved nitrate below the active root zone, and how much nitrogen the crop had already taken up. Check field patterns and soil moisture or ponding, and use a locally calibrated in-season soil nitrate test where that test is valid before deciding whether supplemental nitrogen is justified.
source: Purdue Extension, Should Supplemental Nitrogen be Applied to Corn following Heavy Rainfall? https://ag.purdue.edu/news/department/agry/kernel-news/2021/07/supplemental-n-corn-heavy-rain.html; University of Minnesota Extension, Tips for Accurate Pre-Sidedress Nitrate Tests https://blog-crop-news.extension.umn.edu/2017/06/tips-for-accurate-pre-sidedress-nitrate.html

title: Soil sampling quality
text: Soil sampling should record depth, timing, sampling pattern, lab method, field boundary, management zone, and unusual areas. Recommendation quality is limited by sampling design and local calibration, not just by the model reading a ppm value.

title: Retrieval answer discipline
text: When retrieved agronomic context is incomplete, the agent should identify the missing data, avoid inventing numeric rates, and propose the next measurement, scouting step, or label lookup that would make the recommendation defensible.

title: Conceptual answer mode
text: When the user asks for exam review, a checklist, or a general concept rather than a field-specific recommendation, answer the concept directly first. Add caveats briefly, but do not convert the whole answer into missing-data intake.

title: Hybrid and variety selection factors
text: Hybrid and variety selection should consider relative maturity, local multi-year trial performance, planting date, soil and drainage fit, disease and insect resistance, herbicide or trait package, standability, drydown, lodging risk, seed quality, and field history. Headline single-location yield is not enough.

title: Crop establishment risk checks
text: Planting decisions should check soil temperature, moisture, forecast, seedbed condition, compaction, sidewall smearing risk, residue, planting depth, seed-to-soil contact, and expected emergence uniformity. Finishing early is not useful if establishment risk is high.

title: Precision agriculture records and audit trail
text: Applied information technologies should support recommendations through clean records, georeferenced boundaries, calibrated monitors, validated yield maps, as-applied layers, soil test points, imagery metadata, outlier handling, and an audit trail from data to decision.

title: Manure credits and tile-drained nitrogen planning
text: Nitrogen planning after manure should account for manure analysis, application rate and timing, incorporation, prior crop credits, soil organic matter, realistic yield goal, spring soil nitrate where locally used, tile-drainage loss risk, and split-application timing. Do not ignore manure credits or tile-drainage leaching risk.

title: Lime recommendation inputs
text: A lime recommendation needs soil pH, buffer pH or lab lime requirement, target pH for the crop rotation, soil texture or CEC context, lime source quality such as calcium carbonate equivalent or effective neutralizing value, fineness, incorporation depth, and timing.

title: High soil phosphorus and water quality
text: When soil-test phosphorus is very high near surface water, reduce or avoid additional phosphorus applications, evaluate erosion and runoff pathways, use buffers and setbacks, account for manure history, draw down with crop removal where appropriate, and preserve water-quality risk in the recommendation.

title: Sulfur deficiency triage
text: Sulfur deficiency risk is higher on sandy, low-organic-matter soils after heavy rainfall or irrigation. Confirm field pattern, crop stage, soil and tissue tests where useful, and distinguish sulfur from nitrogen or compaction problems before recommending a sulfur source or rate.

title: Salinity and sodicity evaluation
text: Patchy stunting, white crusting, and poor infiltration in irrigated fields should trigger checks for soil electrical conductivity, sodium adsorption ratio, exchangeable sodium percentage, irrigation-water quality, drainage, leaching fraction, water table, and salt-sensitive crop stage.

title: Traffic compaction diagnostics
text: Traffic-aligned yield strips should be evaluated with yield maps, traffic maps, soil moisture at diagnosis, penetrometer or probe resistance, soil pits, rooting depth, bulk density if available, and depth of restriction. Management can include controlled traffic, avoiding wet traffic, cover crops, and targeted tillage only when conditions justify it.

title: Drainage and wet-spot workflow
text: Persistent wet spots require topography, soil survey or map-unit context, tile maps and outlets, water table or restrictive layer evidence, permeability, rainfall history, field access constraints, and wetland or drainage regulations before suggesting drainage changes.

title: Cover crop water tradeoffs
text: In dryland systems, cover crops can reduce erosion and improve residue cover but may use spring soil moisture. Species, seeding date, termination timing, rainfall outlook, soil water storage, herbicide restrictions, and next crop planting window determine whether the cover crop is a net benefit.

title: Fungicide return-on-investment decision
text: A fungicide pass should be based on scouting, disease identification and severity, crop stage, hybrid or variety susceptibility, weather favorability, yield potential, product label, application cost, crop price, and probability of yield response. Price alone is not a sufficient reason to spray.

title: Insecticide seed treatment risk decision
text: Seed-treatment decisions should consider early planting, cool wet soils, pest history, seedcorn maggot, bean leaf beetle, wireworm or grub risk, residue or manure history, seed cost, stand-loss tolerance, and whether the treatment targets the likely pest. Avoid always-or-never recommendations.

title: Photo diagnosis boundary
text: A single phone photo is rarely enough for a product recommendation. Ask for crop, growth stage, field history, distribution pattern, upper and lower leaf symptoms, recent weather, multiple images, and physical samples if needed. Diagnose first, then check label and threshold before treatment.

title: Replant decision workflow
text: A replant decision should start with stand counts across representative areas, plant survival and growing point health, uniformity and gap length, original planting date, current calendar date, hybrid or variety maturity, expected yield potential of the existing stand, replant costs, seed availability, and weather forecast.

title: Soybean white mold variety and canopy management
text: Fields with white mold history should prioritize variety tolerance ratings, canopy management, row spacing, seeding rate, rotation, irrigation and humidity risk, flowering-period weather, fungicide timing where warranted, and field history. Single-plot headline yield should not override disease risk.

title: Wet corn harvest and storage risk
text: High-moisture corn harvest decisions should address grain moisture, drying capacity and cost, dryer settings, test weight, standability, field loss, mold or mycotoxin risk, aeration, storage time, temperature, and marketing options. Wet grain should not be stored without a drying and aeration plan.

title: Prescription profitability check
text: A variable-rate prescription that increases spend should be checked against soil-test zones, expected yield response, response curves where available, fertilizer and crop prices, application cost, partial budget, check strips or trials, and uncertainty. More fertilizer spend is not automatically more profit.

title: Phone-only yellow crop extension response
text: A phone description of yellow corn or other yellowing crop after heavy rain is not enough to diagnose. Ask for field pattern, crop stage, soil moisture and drainage, recent rainfall, nitrogen and sulfur history, soil test or tissue test, and photos or scouting notes before recommending a fertilizer, pesticide, or rescue treatment.

title: Planting-window establishment decision
text: Before supporting a planting window, check soil temperature at seeding depth, soil moisture or wet-dry field condition, seedbed fitness, sidewall compaction or smearing risk, short forecast, frost or heat stress, seed-to-soil contact, planting depth, and expected emergence or stand risk. A spray window or calendar pressure should not override establishment conditions.

title: Cover-crop moisture and termination tradeoffs
text: Cover-crop decisions before the next cash crop should balance water use and soil moisture, erosion control, residue cover, species or mix, seeding date, crop rotation, termination timing and termination plan, herbicide carryover or restrictions, rainfall outlook, irrigation capacity, and the next-crop planting window. Dry or limited-irrigation regions need an explicit stored-water check.

title: Cross-crop fungicide ROI decision
text: For corn, soybean, canola, sugar beet, grass seed, rice, and other crops, a fungicide pass should not be justified by commodity price alone. Check disease level or scouting severity, pathogen identification, hybrid or variety susceptibility, crop growth stage, weather favorability, yield potential, product label fit, application timing, cost, and probability of yield response.

title: MLRA 063B dryland soil and climate context
text: For a dryland field in MLRA 063B, regional context should connect climate and precipitation limits with soil texture, residue cover, runoff pathways, slope position, and erosion risk. Ask for the field location, landscape position, ecological site or soil map unit, recent rainfall, ground cover, tillage history, and observed rill or wind erosion before turning regional context into management advice.
